strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient video understanding and visual token compression for multimodal LLMs.
The proposed retrieve-then-compress pipeline combining event-based video segmentation, memory retrieval, and RL post-training is conceptually plausible and practically motivated.
The paper reports experiments on six video benchmarks and includes efficiency measurements such as GPU memory and generation latency, which are useful for assessing practical deployment.
The C-GRPO retention-aware reward is an interesting adaptation of GRPO for encouraging a compressed student model to match a full-frame teacher.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited and the wording overstates the contribution: the actual token compression layer is largely a training-free cosine-similarity frame merging heuristic, while C-GRPO trains the LLM rather than learning a token-selection/compression policy. The claim of a 'first post-training RL strategy specifically designed for video token compression' is not supported.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the effect of compression from retrieval. In the ablation, VMR alone with 64 frames achieves mean 45.56, while the final MARC-3B achieves 42.20. This undermines the central claim that the combined retrieval+RL compression framework yields superior performance; it may instead be trading accuracy for aggressive token reduction, but the paper does not frame it that way.

The main 'nearly identical mean performance' claim (42.20 vs 42.21) is fragile and hides large benchmark-specific regressions: VideoMME drops from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55, while TempCompass jumps from 38.05 to 55.34. Averaging such heterogeneous shifts without variance, statistical tests, or per-task discussion is not convincing.

Potential benchmark contamination is not addressed. Training uses Video-R1-260K / Video-R1-COT-style data, and the unusually large TempCompass gain raises concerns about overlap or task-specific fitting. The paper should document decontamination and per-benchmark overlap checks.

Ablations and reproducibility are insufficient. There is no sensitivity analysis for retrieval top-k, compression ratio, event segmentation quality, retrieval accuracy, memory-bank size, or the compression layer without C-GRPO. Implementation details such as query embedding, retrieval training, event detector, prompts, hyperparameters, and code are largely missing.

Efficiency claims are not fully supported end-to-end. The reported 72% memory reduction and 23.9% generation-latency reduction are notable, but the end-to-end single-sample latency reduction is only 11.1%, and the paper does not account for the overhead of VMR segmentation, embedding, and retrieval in the deployment pipeline.

The paper makes broad deployment claims for autonomous driving, surveillance, and real-time QA without evidence under those settings, and some key implementation details are deferred to missing appendices, limiting reproducibility and the strength of the conclusions.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient video understanding via token compression.
Combines retrieval (VMR) with compression and RL-based post-training, and evaluates on six video benchmarks.
Reports substantial reductions in visual tokens, GPU memory, and generation latency, which are practically relevant if valid.
Includes some ablation studies on VMR and the threshold tau, and compares against several existing compression methods.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is technically flawed: the compression reward r_c = alpha * max(0, eta - tau) is gated by correctness and, for a given query, a_comp and a_full are constant across the group. After group-relative advantage normalization (Eq. 9), this constant term cancels out and has no effect on the policy gradient beyond standard GRPO with a correctness reward. Thus the claimed retention alignment / distillation mechanism is likely a no-op, and the main novelty is unsupported.

The VMR is severely under-specified: event segmentation network, embedding model, contrastive training, query representation, retrieval indexing, and hyperparameters are all vague or missing, making the method impossible to reproduce.

The evaluation is unfair and selectively framed. VMR alone with 64 frames achieves 45.56 mean, substantially higher than the 64-frame Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline (42.21) and higher than MARC (42.20). The paper compares MARC to the weaker uniform-sampling baseline while omitting that the retrieval component alone already beats the baseline, so gains are largely attributable to retrieval, not compression or C-GRPO.

Efficiency claims ignore the computational overhead of VMR. Event detection, embedding extraction, and nearest-neighbor retrieval over the full video are not included in GPU memory or latency measurements. The reported 72% memory reduction and 23.9% generation latency reduction are therefore not end-to-end and may be misleading.

The claim of using 'one frame's worth of tokens' is inconsistent with the reported token counts: 122.69 tokens is about 4.71% of 2589.93 tokens, i.e., roughly 3 frames' worth at the baseline's average of ~40 tokens/frame. This overstates the compression level and undermines the main claim.

Missing critical ablations: there is no comparison of C-GRPO against standard GRPO on the same data, no VMR+compression without C-GRPO under identical training data, and no controlled comparison of C-GRPO versus SFT on the same training set. The SFT baseline uses different data (10K from Video-R1-COT-165K) than C-GRPO (5K from Video-R1-260K), so the claimed +9.6% gain is not apples-to-apples.

Novelty is limited. The compression layer is essentially a variant of MovieChat-style cosine-similarity frame merging, and C-GRPO is a minor modification of GRPO. The paper's claim of being the 'first' RL post-training strategy for video token compression is not convincingly established.

The paper lacks error bars, significance tests, and sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters such as top-k, alpha, compression ratio rho, and group size G. The tau ablation shows only marginal differences (41.34 vs 42.20 vs 41.40), which may be noise.
Reproducibility is poor: no code, no model weights, no detailed training hyperparameters, no VMR implementation details, and no compute budget for training or retrieval.

The manuscript contains many citation and formatting errors (e.g., mismatched author-year keys, duplicate/incorrect references, inconsistent benchmark names), indicating insufficient care in preparation.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reducing visual token overhead for video LLMs.
Proposes a combined retrieve-then-compress framework (VMR + C-GRPO) that is conceptually reasonable and integrates event-level retrieval with RL-based compression.
Reports extensive experiments on six video benchmarks and multiple baselines, with strong token reduction (95%) and comparable mean accuracy to a 64-frame baseline.
Provides ablation studies on VMR and τ, and efficiency measurements showing substantial GPU memory reduction (72%) and some latency improvement.
The idea of using a retention-aware reward in GRPO for compression is a novel direction worth exploring.
weaknesses: The main accuracy claim is misleading: MARC (42.20) underperforms VMR alone with 64 frames (45.56) on the same benchmarks, often by large margins (e.g., MVBench 45.82 vs 57.24, VideoMME 39.44 vs 51.85). The proper comparison for the full MARC pipeline should be to VMR without compression, not only to the no-retrieval baseline.

C-GRPO is not well specified: it is unclear how the full-frame teacher reward a_full is computed, whether the teacher uses VMR, how the retention reward is integrated during training, and how it avoids reward hacking. The method is essentially GRPO with a gated scalar retention bonus, and its novelty over standard GRPO is limited.

VMR details are insufficient: the embedding model, contrastive training procedure, query encoding, event segmentation parameters, and retrieval accuracy are not described in the main text. No analysis of retrieval quality is provided.

Evaluation has weaknesses: the mean is unweighted across benchmarks and hides large per-benchmark regressions. No weighted mean, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported. The τ ablation shows only small differences (41.34, 42.20, 41.40) without significance testing.

Baseline controls are not fully fair: the SFT baseline uses 10K samples from Video-R1-COT-165K while MARC uses 5K from Video-R1-260K; compression baselines are not clearly matched for token count (some are listed as 64 frames), and recent token compression methods (e.g., VisionZip, SparseVLM) are not compared.

Efficiency analysis excludes the overhead of VMR (event segmentation, embedding, nearest-neighbor retrieval), which may be substantial for long videos. End-to-end latency reduction is only 11.1%, which is modest given the 95% token reduction.

Reproducibility is limited: key hyperparameters such as ρ, m, and N_target are not stated in the main text; no code/weights are mentioned; references contain errors; and the manuscript contains an unresolved 'Appendix ??' placeholder.
Potential benchmark contamination is not addressed: training on Video-R1-260K may include evaluation benchmarks (e.g., TempCompass), which could explain the unusually large gain on TempCompass.

Writing and clarity need improvement: several grammatical issues, undefined notation, and overclaiming (e.g., 'superior results', 'first post-training RL strategy') that is not fully supported by the evidence.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing the computational cost of video VLMs for latency- and resource-constrained deployment.
Proposes a coherent retrieve-then-compress pipeline that combines event-level retrieval with RL-based token compression.
Reports experiments on six video benchmarks and provides efficiency metrics such as GPU memory and generation latency.
Includes useful ablations on the retention threshold tau, VMR, and comparison to SFT-based compression.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the Visual Memory Retriever relies on off-the-shelf event segmentation and retrieval components, while C-GRPO is largely a GRPO variant with an added retention-ratio reward; the claim of being the first RL post-training method for video token compression is not convincingly supported.

Method details are insufficient for reproducibility: the event segmentation model, embedding model, contrastive training objective, query representation, nearest-neighbor index, VMR training procedure, and top-k sensitivity are not adequately described.

C-GRPO formulation is unclear: it is not specified how the full-frame and compressed rewards a_full and a_comp are computed per sample/group, whether the teacher is fixed, how retention is estimated during online RL, or how the gated compression reward avoids reward hacking.

Evaluation has fairness and baseline concerns: VMR alone with 64 frames achieves a higher mean (45.56) than MARC with 1 frame (42.20), so the headline 'nearly identical' result is relative to the weaker uncompressed baseline rather than the stronger VMR baseline. SFT and C-GRPO also use different dataset sizes and sources, and baseline reproductions are not fully specified.

The large TempCompass gain (38.05 to 55.34) is unusually large and may be due to prompt, training-data, or evaluation-protocol differences rather than token compression alone; this needs stronger validation.

Efficiency claims omit the cost of VMR: event segmentation, embedding extraction, and retrieval overhead are not included in the reported memory or latency numbers, and end-to-end latency reduction is only 11.1%.
Long-video performance is weak: VideoMME drops from 53.55 to 39.44, which undermines the broad deployment claims for long or real-time video understanding.
Reproducibility is weak: no code or detailed implementation is provided, and key hyperparameters, retrieval details, reward computation, and training data sampling are missing.

Writing and formatting issues reduce clarity: inconsistent notation (e.g., H vs h), unclear figure/equation references, and reference-list formatting errors make the technical presentation harder to follow.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient video understanding and visual token compression for VLMs.
Proposes a combined retrieve-then-compress framework (VMR + C-GRPO) with a cognitively inspired event-segmentation/retrieval pipeline.
Evaluates on six video benchmarks and reports large token reduction (~95%), memory savings (~72%), and some efficiency gains.
Includes ablations on the retention threshold τ and comparisons to SFT and VMR-only variants, providing partial evidence for the proposed components.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely combines existing ideas—event segmentation, retrieval, cosine-similarity frame merging, and GRPO—with C-GRPO being a relatively small reward modification. The memory-aware compression layer is essentially averaging frames, and the claim of being the 'first' RL strategy for video token compression is overstrong and insufficiently supported.

Misleading comparison and evaluation: the main claim of parity with the 64-frame baseline relies on mean performance, but per-benchmark results show severe degradation on VideoMME (53.55→39.44) and VSI-Bench (32.93→27.55), offset by a large TempCompass gain. More importantly, VMR alone with 64 frames achieves 45.56 mean, higher than MARC's 42.20, so the full method does not maintain performance relative to its own uncompressed retrieval-augmented version. The baseline is also not trained, while MARC uses RL post-training, confounding compression with training gains.

Missing baselines: only three older training-free compression methods are compared. There is no comparison to recent token compression/efficient video LLM methods (e.g., VisionZip, SparseVLM, TokenPacker, FastV, LLaVA-OneVision) or to training-based compression approaches.

Potential data contamination: training uses 5K samples from Video-R1-260K, which may overlap with evaluation benchmarks such as VideoMMMU, MVBench, and TempCompass. No contamination analysis or discussion is provided, making the reported gains difficult to interpret.

Method underspecified: key details are missing, including the compression ratio ρ, N_target, how the final one-frame token count is achieved from top-k retrieved segments, and the exact cross-segment merging procedure. C-GRPO reward computation is unclear: how a_full (teacher reward) is computed per query, whether η is per-sample or group-level, what r_i includes, and how the teacher is used during training. The value of α is not reported. Notation is inconsistent (e.g., H vs H_t, h_i ∈ R^d vs R^{P×d}).

Weak ablation: only τ and VMR/SFT comparisons are provided. There is no ablation of the memory-aware compression layer, top-k retrieval, event segmentation, reward gating, or KL term. Differences across τ are small (41.34, 42.20, 41.40) and lack statistical significance or error bars.

Efficiency claims are overstated: the highlighted 23.9% generation latency reduction corresponds to only 11.1% end-to-end latency reduction. Retrieval and compression overhead are not reported, so practical speedup remains unclear.

Reproducibility is insufficient: despite the statement that code will be released, no link is provided. Key hyperparameters (ρ, α, N_target, C-GRPO training hardware, VMR embedding/segmentation details, retrieval index construction) are missing.

Clarity and writing issues: typos and confusing figure captions; 'ordered group size' likely means 'group size'; several overclaims such as 'nearly identical', 'robust solution', and 'for the first time' are not fully supported by the evidence.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: efficient video understanding via visual token compression, with potential deployment benefits in latency- and memory-constrained settings.
Combines event-level retrieval (VMR) with an RL-based compression/distillation strategy (C-GRPO), which is a reasonably novel direction for video token compression.
Evaluates on six diverse video benchmarks covering both reasoning and general understanding, and reports efficiency metrics such as token reduction, GPU memory, and latency.
Provides ablations on the retention threshold tau and comparisons against SFT and VMR variants, giving some insight into component contributions.
The paper is generally well organized and the motivation from cognitive science/event segmentation is clearly presented.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not apples-to-apples. MARC uses VMR at inference, but the 64-frame Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline does not. VMR alone with 64 frames achieves 45.56 mean accuracy, higher than MARC's 42.20, so MARC does not match the strongest 64-frame baseline; it trades accuracy for efficiency. The abstract's claim of 'nearly identical accuracy to the 64-frame baseline' is therefore misleading.

The C-GRPO distillation objective is weak. The only substantive addition is a gated compression reward based on a group-average retention ratio; there is no token-level or output-matching distillation loss that directly transfers teacher reasoning. It is also unclear how a_full and a_comp are computed, whether the teacher is frozen, and how the reward is assigned per sample.

The Visual Memory Retriever (VMR) is severely underdescribed. There are no details on training the contrastive embedding space, query representation, event segmentation parameters, retrieval training data, or retrieval accuracy, making the method difficult to reproduce.

Missing ablation: there is no comparison of VMR + compression without C-GRPO (or VMR + simple compression) to isolate the effect of C-GRPO. The main table also omits the VMR 64-frame baseline, which is the relevant upper bound for the retrieval-augmented setting.

Compression details are incomplete. The short-term memory window length m, the compression ratio rho, how the final single-frame token representation is formed across segments, and how temporal information is preserved are not specified.

Efficiency claims are selective. The abstract highlights a 23.9% generation latency reduction, but the reported end-to-end latency reduction is only 11.1%, and VMR retrieval/segmentation overhead is not measured or included in the efficiency analysis.

Training uses only 5K samples with no stability curves, statistical significance tests, or comparison to other RL fine-tuning baselines. Comparisons to larger off-the-shelf models (InternVL3.5-4B, Gemma-3-4B) are not meaningful because those models are not fine-tuned on the same video QA data.

Some claims are overstatements. C-GRPO is described as the 'first' RL strategy for video token compression, but it is a relatively minor modification of GRPO. The paper also inconsistently names methods/baselines (e.g., DynamicVLM vs. ByteVideoLLM, MARC-3B vs. MARC-3B-0.6, VideoMMU vs. VideoMMMU).
